story: Wrangell–St. Elias rises from the sea to 18,008 feet at Mount Saint Elias, the second-highest peak in the United States and Canada, less than ten miles from tidewater. The park takes in the entire Wrangell range, much of the Saint Elias Mountains and the eastern Chugach. With its preserve, it is about the size of Yellowstone, Yosemite and Switzerland combined.

Volcanoes and ice have shaped it. Mount Wrangell is a massive shield volcano that still steams. The Malaspina Glacier is the largest piedmont glacier in North America, spreading out across the coastal plain; the Hubbard Glacier is the longest tidewater glacier in Alaska; and the Nabesna is the longest valley glacier in the world.

The Ahtna have lived along the Copper River for about a thousand years, and the Upper Tanana, Eyak and Tlingit live around the park's edges. They used pure copper for tools, which drew Russian explorers in search of it. From the early 1900s, the mines at Kennecott worked one of the world's richest copper deposits, linked to the coast by a 195-mile railway, until they closed in 1938.

President Jimmy Carter proclaimed a national monument in 1978, and the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act made it a national park and preserve in 1980. With Canada's Kluane and neighbouring parks it forms one of the largest protected areas on Earth, a World Heritage Site since 1979. Local rural residents still hunt and fish for subsistence in the park.

sightNotes.poi-wrangell-st-elias-kennecott-mines: The red mill town of the copper mines, with ranger-led and guided tours of the fourteen-storey concentration mill.
sightNotes.poi-wrangell-st-elias-root-glacier: A trail from Kennecott to the edge of the glacier. Walking on the ice needs crampons, or a guide.
sightNotes.poi-wrangell-st-elias-mccarthy-road: Sixty miles of gravel from Chitina along an old railbed, ending at a footbridge to McCarthy.
sightNotes.poi-wrangell-st-elias-nabesna-road: A 42-mile gravel road into the park's northern foothills, with trails, campsites and views of the Wrangells.
sightNotes.poi-wrangell-st-elias-crystalline-hills-: A short hike off the McCarthy Road with views of the Chugach and Wrangell mountains.
sightNotes.poi-wrangell-st-elias-malaspina-glacier: The largest piedmont glacier in North America, best seen from the air or from Yakutat.
sightNotes.poi-wrangell-st-elias-mount-saint-elias: The park's highest summit, on the Canadian border, rising from near sea level to 18,008 feet.
sightNotes.poi-wrangell-st-elias-mount-wrangell: A huge, gently sloped shield volcano whose summit vents still steam.

entrances: The main visitor center is at Copper Center on the Richardson Highway, about 200 miles east of Anchorage
McCarthy Road — from Chitina, 60 miles of gravel to the Kennicott River footbridge; walk or take a shuttle on to McCarthy and Kennecott
Nabesna Road — from Slana, on the Tok Cut-Off
Air taxis fly into the park from McCarthy, Glennallen and other towns
permits: Backcountry trips need no permit, but leaving a trip plan with the park is strongly advised
lodging: Lodges in McCarthy and Kennecott, on private land
Kendesnii Campground on the Nabesna Road, and public-use cabins
seasonalClosures: Most services, shuttles and tours run from late May to early September
The gravel roads can be rough and slow; check rental car rules before driving them
camping: Kendesnii Campground, first come, first served

chronology.text: Vitus Bering's expedition reaches the coast.
President Jimmy Carter proclaims Wrangell–St. Elias National Monument.
The area is named a World Heritage Site with Canada's Kluane.
The Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act creates the national park and preserve.

safety: Glaciers have crevasses and moulins. Don't walk on ice without crampons and experience, or a guide.
Rivers are cold, fast and braided. Cross only where you are sure, and never alone.
This is bear country. Carry bear spray and store food properly.
regulations: Much of the land along the roads is private. Respect closed signs and mining claims.
Respect subsistence camps, fish wheels and equipment.

fees.title: Entrance
fees.detail: Fee Free Park: Visitors can access the Headquarters Visitor Center in Copper Center in summer (mid-May through mid-September). Gate open for day use only 9 am - 5 pm. Access to Nabesna Road and McCarthy Road open year-round, weather dependent. Summer can have heavy rains and impassable streams. Fall - Winter - Spring can have deep snow after storms. The gravel park roads are owned and maintained by the Alaska State Dept of Transportation - grading in summer and snow plowing in winter are infrequent. Parking and camping fees are possible at privately owned businesses permitted to operate in the park. --There is private overnight parking and camping for a fee at mile 60 at the Kennicott River Bridge, 1/2 mile west of McCarthy town.

operatingHours: The park and public lands are always open but visitor facilities have limited seasons: Open in Summer. Call ahead for hours: Copper Center (907) 822-7250, Slana (907) 822-7401, Chitina (907) 823-7250 and Kennecott (907) 205-7106. CLOSED Mid-September through April.
weather: Varies widely depending on location in park and time of year. Visit https://www.nps.gov/wrst/planyourvisit/weather.htm for detailed information.
directions: The administrative building and main park visitor center are located along the Richardson Highway (Hwy 4), which is a paved state highway that runs through Copper Center, AK. The buildings are 8 miles south of the Glenn Highway and Richardson Highway intersection near Glennallen, Alaska. This is approximately 200 miles east of Anchorage, AK and 250 miles south of Fairbanks, AK.
